title: Preliminary incident report: DSV Cormorant, dive 214
text:
# Preliminary incident report: DSV Cormorant, dive 214

Filed by the Dive Operations Officer, 3 November.

At 09:42 local time on 2 November, the deep submergence vehicle Cormorant
departed the support ship Halvard Lyng for a routine survey of the Kestrel Rise,
a basalt ridge in the eastern basin. The dive plan called for four hours at a
working depth of 1,850 metres, with two hours of transit either side. Aboard
were pilot Ines Okonkwo, co-pilot Tobias Reiner, and observer Dr Amara Sell.

Descent was normal. At 11:14, passing 1,610 metres, the vehicle reported a
transient dropout on the primary power bus lasting approximately 400
milliseconds. The crew logged it and continued. A second dropout at 11:31 lasted
just over two seconds and took the forward thrusters and the primary lighting
array offline. Both recovered without intervention.

At 11:58, at a depth of 1,844 metres, the primary bus failed entirely. The
vehicle transferred to the reserve bus as designed. The reserve bus carries life
support, communications, and the ballast release, but not propulsion. Cormorant
was at that point neutrally buoyant and drifting at approximately 0.3 knots on
the prevailing current.

The crew followed the standard procedure and released the descent weights at
12:04. Ascent began at roughly 22 metres per minute. Cormorant surfaced at 13:31
approximately 4.1 nautical miles east of the Halvard Lyng and was recovered at
14:52. No injuries were sustained. Dr Sell reported a headache consistent with
the elevated carbon dioxide observed in the final forty minutes of ascent.

The vehicle was recovered intact. Initial inspection found no hull breach and no
water ingress in the pressure sphere. The cause of the bus failure was not
determined at the time of filing and is referred to Engineering.

This report is preliminary. It records what was observed and does not attempt to
assign a cause.

title: Engineering findings: primary bus failure, DSV Cormorant
text:
# Engineering findings: primary bus failure, DSV Cormorant

To the Dive Operations Officer, 19 November. From the Vehicle Systems group.

We have completed teardown of the primary power distribution assembly recovered
from dive 214. The failure originated in the starboard penetrator block, at the
junction where the main bus passes from the pressure sphere into the wet bay.

The penetrator uses a compression seal against a machined titanium seat. On
disassembly we found the seat scored along roughly a third of its circumference.
The scoring is consistent with a hard particle trapped during the seal
replacement carried out in the August maintenance period. Under pressure the
compression seal deformed into the scoring, opening a path for seawater to reach
the conductor. Resistance across the junction rose as salt deposits accumulated,
which accounts for the two transient dropouts before the full failure.

We want to be plain about the sequence. This was not a sudden failure. The
vehicle gave two warnings, seventeen minutes apart, and the second one took
propulsion offline for two seconds at 1,610 metres. Under the procedures in
force at the time, neither warning obliged the crew to abort. We think that is
the finding that matters, more than the seal itself.

The August maintenance period was carried out at sea rather than in the shore
facility, following the schedule compression agreed after the Kestrel Rise
survey was brought forward. Seal replacement at sea is permitted under the
maintenance manual. It is performed in the wet bay, which is not a clean
environment.

Recommendations. First, penetrator seal work should be restricted to the shore
facility. Second, any transient on the primary bus exceeding one second should
be a mandatory abort. Third, the reserve bus should carry sufficient power for
station-keeping, so that a vehicle on reserve is not obliged to surface blind
under whatever current it happens to be in.

title: Review board findings: dive 214
text:
# Review board findings: dive 214

Adopted 8 December. The board comprised three members, none of whom belonged to
the Vehicle Systems group or to Dive Operations.

The board accepts the Engineering account of the mechanism. A scored penetrator
seat admitted seawater to the starboard bus junction; accumulating salt deposits
raised resistance until the bus failed. We do not restate that analysis here.

The board's concern is different. Cormorant gave two warnings before it failed,
and the procedures in force did not require the crew to act on either. The
second transient took propulsion offline for two seconds at 1,610 metres. Had
the full failure occurred at that moment rather than twenty-seven minutes later,
the vehicle would have been in the same condition it was ultimately in — on
reserve power, without propulsion — but 234 metres shallower and closer to the
ridge wall. The board regards the outcome of dive 214 as substantially a matter
of where the vehicle happened to be.

On the maintenance decision, the board finds that performing penetrator seal
work at sea was permitted, was not unusual, and had been done four times in the
preceding two years without incident. The board declines to treat the August
work as an error. It notes instead that a procedure permitting work in a
non-clean environment, with no post-work verification of the seat, tolerates a
failure mode it has no way to detect.

The board makes two findings. The programme's schedule compression, agreed in
June, removed the shore maintenance window that would otherwise have applied.
And the abort criteria in force were written around events rather than around
warnings, which is why two warnings produced no obligation.

The board endorses all three of the Engineering recommendations and adds a
fourth: that abort criteria be reviewed by someone outside the operating group,
annually.

title: Pilot's log, dive 214
text:
# Pilot's log, dive 214

Ines Okonkwo, transcribed from the voice record.

0942. Away clean. Sea state two. Tobias has the descent.

1015. Passing 800. Water is very clear today, clearer than the last three dives.
We are seeing the thermocline as a shimmer rather than a wall.

1114. Sixteen ten. We had a flicker on the main bus, under half a second.
Everything came back on its own. Logged it. Tobias says he has seen worse on the
older vehicles. Continuing.

1131. Sixteen ten again, holding for the survey line. Second flicker and this
one had teeth — two seconds, and it took the forward thrusters and the main
lights with it. We were dark and drifting for those two seconds. Amara did not
say anything, which is how I know it was bad. Everything came back.

I want to say here that I thought about calling it. The procedure does not
require an abort for a transient. I read the criteria twice on the way down and
they are written around things that have already happened. A flicker is not a
listed event. I decided that twice is a pattern and I would call it if there was
a third.

1158. Eighteen forty-four. Third one, and it did not come back. Main bus gone.
We are on reserve. Life support good, comms good, no thrust.

1204. Weights away. We are going up.

1230. Passing 1100. Steady, about twenty-two a minute. Amara is doing the
breathing exercise. CO2 is climbing but inside limits.

1315. Passing 300. I can see the light change.

1331. Surfaced. We are a long way east of the ship. Nothing to do about that
without thrusters — you go up where the water takes you.

1452. Aboard. Everyone walked out.

Note for the debrief: the criteria are wrong. Not the seal, whatever they find.
The criteria. We were given two warnings and told we did not need to listen.

title: Maintenance record extract: DSV Cormorant, August period
text:
# Maintenance record extract: DSV Cormorant, August period

Compiled for the review board, 27 November.

The August maintenance period ran from 4 to 11 August aboard the Halvard Lyng,
at sea, on station over the eastern basin. The period was originally scheduled
for the shore facility at Vardstrand from 12 to 26 August. It was moved after
the Kestrel Rise survey was brought forward by six weeks, a decision recorded in
the programme change note of 14 June.

Work carried out in the period included: replacement of both penetrator
compression seals, port and starboard; inspection of the ballast release
mechanism; replacement of two thruster bearings; recharge and load test of the
reserve bus batteries; and routine hull survey.

The penetrator seal replacement is recorded as completed on 7 August by two
technicians, signed off the same day. The maintenance manual requires visual
inspection of the seat before the new seal is fitted. That inspection is
recorded as performed. The manual does not require the seat to be measured, and
no measurement was taken. Nor does it require photographic record, and none
exists.

The wet bay was not a controlled environment during the period. The record notes
that seal work was carried out with the bay open to the deck, which is standard
practice at sea, and that the sea state during the period ranged from two to
four.

Four previous penetrator seal replacements were carried out at sea in the
preceding two years: in October, the following March, that June, and the
following February. None was followed by a reported bus anomaly.

The shore facility at Vardstrand has a clean bench rated for this work. The
programme has used it for penetrator work on eleven occasions since the vehicle
entered service.
